question: Why are checkouts failing?
options: Postgres CPU saturated by sale traffic, refusing new work
Connection leak in checkout-api holding sessions open
New pods × per-pod pool size now exceed max_connections
Slow queries holding connections longer under load

explanation.cause: Autoscaling to 40 pods × 20 conns asks for 800 sessions; Postgres allows 500.
explanation.why: Every pod opens its own pool straight to Postgres. Past ~25 pods the fleet can request more backends than max_connections, so new connections are refused with SQLSTATE 53300. The database isn’t busy — it’s out of slots. Fix with a pooler (PgBouncer) or cap pool size × maxReplicas.
explanation.tell: Errors start as replicas pass 25 — and 25 × 20 = 500 — while DB CPU sits flat at 31% and nothing has shipped in 3 days.

question: What is starving ledger of connections?
options: Slow queries holding connections; the DB can’t keep up
Connections leaked on an error path that never closes them
maximumPoolSize too small for current request volume
Open transactions holding row locks and blocking others

explanation.cause: A failure path added in v3.18 checks out a connection and never returns it.
explanation.why: When the fx-rates call fails after a connection is borrowed, the new retry wrapper throws before close() runs. Each failure strands one connection; Hikari never reclaims it, so active creeps up in steps until all 20 are pinned and every request waits 30s for a slot.
explanation.tell: Active climbs stepwise at flat traffic and never falls, while Postgres sees those 20 sessions as plain idle for hours — a full pool in front of an idle database.

question: Why is all traffic to orders stuck?
options: ADD COLUMN is rewriting the whole orders table on disk
Row-lock contention from the evening checkout write burst
Autovacuum on orders is holding a conflicting table lock
ALTER waits on a long query; everything queues behind it

explanation.cause: ALTER TABLE queued behind a 47-min report query; all traffic queued behind it.
explanation.why: ALTER TABLE needs ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, so it waits for pid 2988’s ACCESS SHARE lock. Postgres queues every later lock request on orders behind the pending ALTER — even plain SELECTs. Run DDL with a short lock_timeout so it fails fast and retries instead of freezing the table.
explanation.tell: The ALTER is waiting, not running, and every waiter names the same holder — 2988, a 47-min BI report query — with the ALTER first in the queue. CPU drops: nothing can run.

question: Tap the line that explains why new orders 404.

explanation.cause: A long query on the replica is blocking WAL replay, so replica reads are minutes stale.
explanation.why: Replay reached a vacuum cleanup record removing rows a replica query’s snapshot still needs. With max_standby_streaming_delay = -1 the startup process waits forever instead of canceling the query, so replay stops and every read routed to the replica sees pre-09:31 data.
explanation.tell: The replica’s startup process logs a snapshot conflict wait at the exact moment lag starts climbing in a straight line — while WAL is still received in 0.3s. Replay is paused, not slow.

question: Why can’t autovacuum get ledger out of this?
options: An orphaned prepared transaction pins the xmin horizon
autovacuum_max_workers too low to freeze big tables in time
A hot_standby_feedback replica slot is holding back xmin
A long-running session transaction is blocking freezing

explanation.cause: A 63-day-old prepared transaction stops vacuum from freezing anything newer than it.
explanation.why: Vacuum can only freeze tuples older than the oldest XID still visible to someone. A prepared (2PC) transaction survives restarts and disconnects, so xid 1871203 pins the horizon ~2.14B XIDs back. Autovacuum keeps running and can’t advance relfrozenxid; ROLLBACK PREPARED it, then VACUUM.
explanation.tell: The vacuum’s removable cutoff (1871203) is exactly the prepared transaction’s XID. The slot’s xmin and the oldest session are recent, so they can’t be the anchor.

question: What’s burning the database CPU?
options: Autoanalyze after the deploy left bad planner statistics
Connection storm from pods restarting during the rollout
New query filters on an unindexed column, so it seq-scans
Cache stampede after the rollout flushed every pod cache

explanation.cause: v5.12 queries orders by customer_email, which no index covers.
explanation.why: With no index on customer_email, every guest order lookup reads all 48M rows and sorts the matches. Each takes ~3s of CPU and I/O, and at request volume that pins the box. Fix with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on (customer_email, created_at).
explanation.tell: CPU jumps at the 14:06 release, every slow query is the same new statement filtering on customer_email, and seq_scans on orders go from 3 to 410 per minute.

question: What is filling the database volume?
options: archive_command failing, so old WAL can’t be recycled
An inactive replication slot is pinning WAL since Tuesday
Table bloat from autovacuum falling behind on orders
max_wal_size raised too high in the last config push

explanation.cause: The CDC connector died and its logical slot has retained every WAL segment since.
explanation.why: A replication slot guarantees WAL is kept until its consumer confirms it. With the consumer gone and max_slot_wal_keep_size unlimited, Postgres can’t remove any segment after restart_lsn, so pg_wal grows with every write until the disk fills.
explanation.tell: All growth is in pg_wal, not table data; the archiver is healthy; the slot is inactive and the growth starts right when the connector failed on Tuesday night.

question: Tap the line that shows why job_queue keeps bloating.

explanation.cause: A session idle in transaction since 13:02 stops vacuum from removing dead queue rows.
explanation.why: A queue table churns constantly. Vacuum may only remove rows deleted before the oldest open snapshot, and reconcile-cron opened one at 13:02 and never committed. Autovacuum runs fine but frees nothing, so dequeue scans millions of dead tuples for 18k live ones.
explanation.tell: Vacuum completed and removed 0 tuples, with 2.9M ‘dead but not yet removable’. The canceled autovacuum is a red herring — the next run finished and still couldn’t clean.

question: Tap the line that explains the 500s.

explanation.cause: Reservations lock the same SKUs in opposite order and deadlock each other.
explanation.why: ord_51Ka locks SKU-1182 then wants SKU-0457; ord_51Kb holds SKU-0457 and wants SKU-1182. After deadlock_timeout (1s) Postgres aborts one transaction. Sort SKUs before locking so every transaction acquires rows in the same order.
explanation.tell: Two reservations for the same SKUs in opposite order arrive 6ms apart; ~1s later one fails. ‘Transaction is aborted’ is fallout from the deadlock, not the cause.

question: Why are writes still failing 17 minutes after the switchover?
options: Pods reconnected to pg-a via cached DNS; pools kept them
pg-b is still in recovery after promotion, rejecting writes
default_transaction_read_only was left on after switchover
Pre-failover connections to pg-a were never evicted

explanation.cause: Pods with stale DNS refilled their pools on pg-a after it came back read-only.
explanation.why: The switchover killed every connection and Hikari refilled pools at once. Pods whose JVM still cached the old IP for up to 60s connected to pg-a, now a replica. Those sessions are healthy, so Hikari keeps them until maxLifetime — every write on them fails with 25006 for up to 30 min.
explanation.tell: Errors are read-only (25006), not connection failures, and confined to 4 pods. Old connections were already evicted at 02:14:06, and the 8 healthy pods prove pg-b takes writes.
